## Overview

The Acehnese, also written as Achinese, are an Austronesian ethnic group native to Aceh, a province on the northernmost tip of Sumatra in Indonesia. Their population is estimated at between 3,526,000 and 4.2 million people; the language article gives around 2.8 million speakers within Aceh according to the 2010 census. Acehnese society traditionally centered on agriculture, metalworking, weaving, and communal life in *gampôngs*, which combine into districts known as *mukims*. The group’s history includes Hindu and Buddhist influences, long interaction with Indian, Arab, Persian, Turkish, Portuguese, Malay, Minangkabau, and other regional populations, and the rise of the Islamic Aceh Sultanate. Acehnese culture is expressed through language, Islamic practice, customary institutions, dance, cuisine, oral poetry, and historical resistance to Portuguese and Dutch colonial conquest.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Weaving** — The sources identify weaving as a traditional occupation of the Acehnese.

### Clothing & dress

The sources state that ancient inhabitants of northernmost Sumatra wore cotton clothing, while the ruling elite wore silk. Acehnese dress is therefore not covered in sufficient detail by the sources used.

### Architecture

The sources identify *gampôngs* as communal settlements that combine into districts known as *mukims*. The sources also mention *Rumoh Aceh* in a “See also” section, but provide no architectural description. Acehnese architecture is otherwise not covered by the sources used.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Metalworking is identified as a traditional Acehnese occupation.

## Music & performance

The sources identify several Acehnese performance forms and name a musical instrument associated with one of them. Traditional Acehnese dance is generally performed in groups, either standing or sitting, with dancers of the same gender. From a musical perspective, dances are divided into forms accompanied by vocals and the dancers’ own physical percussive movements, and forms accompanied by an ensemble of musical instruments.

The named dance and performance traditions are *Laweut*, *Likok Pulo*, *Pho*, *Rabbani Wahed*, *Ranup lam Puan*, *Rapa'i Geleng*, *Rateb Meuseukat*, *Ratoh Duek*, *Seudati*, *Tarek Pukat*, and *Saman*.

Acehnese oral culture also includes *hadih maja*, identified in the source as an oral poem. One such poem is quoted in connection with Snouck Hurgronje’s *De Atjeher*.

## Dance & theatre

Traditional Acehnese dance portrays heritage culture, religion, and the folklore of common people. Performances are generally collective, with dancers arranged in standing or sitting groups and divided by gender. Some dances use vocals and the physical percussion of dancers, while others use an ensemble of musical instruments.

The sources name *Laweut*, *Likok Pulo*, *Pho*, *Rabbani Wahed*, *Ranup lam Puan*, *Rapa'i Geleng*, *Rateb Meuseukat*, *Ratoh Duek*, *Seudati*, *Tarek Pukat*, and *Saman*. Theatre, puppetry, and dramatic traditions are not covered by the sources used.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources describe Acehnese burial practices among the earliest inhabitants of Aceh, who lived during the Pleistocene age and practiced rituals of burial. They also describe the gradual Islamization of Aceh, the major place of Islam in the region by the thirteenth century, and the long-standing predominance of Muslim identity among the Acehnese.

## Foodways

Acehnese cuisine combines spices commonly found in Indian and Arabic cuisine, including ginger, pepper, coriander, cumin, cloves, cinnamon, cardamom, and fennel. Foods are often cooked with curry or curry and coconut milk and combined with buffalo, beef, mutton, fish, or chicken. Some older recipes used cannabis as a flavoring spice, but the source states that these substances are no longer used.

Named Acehnese foods include *Ayam tangkap*, *Bhoi*, *Eungkot paya*, *Kuwah eungkôt yèe*, *Kuah beulangong*, *Kanji rumbi*, *Keumamah*, *Kuwah pliëk-u*, *Martabak aceh*, *Masam keueueng*, *Meuseukat*, *Mie aceh*, *Mie caluk*, *Nasi gurih*, *Roti cane*, *Roti jala*, *Sambai asam udeueng*, *Sate matang*, *Sie reuboh*, *Sop sumsum*, and *Timphan*.

## Oral tradition & literature

Acehnese folklore states that the earliest people of Aceh came from indigenous groups including the Mante people and the Lhan people. The sources describe the Mante people as a local native group believed to be related to the Batak, Gayonese, and Alas people, while the Lhan people are described as allegedly related to the Semang people group.

The oral poem *hadih maja* is cited in connection with Snouck Hurgronje’s *De Atjeher*. Acehnese literature was historically limited because much writing in Aceh was produced in Malay, which functioned as the lingua franca. The earliest written record identified by the source is *Hikayat Sama'un* (“The Story of Syama'un”) from 1658 CE. Acehnese literature consisted mostly of poetry, including *hikayat* and *nazam*, while *Kitab Bakeu Meunan* is identified as a prose translation of *Qawaa'id al-Islaam*.

The sources also describe Dutch efforts to document Acehnese language and literacy traditions, including Snouck Hurgronje’s 1892 study of Acehnese language and script. The Acehnese Wikipedia was launched on August 12, 2009, and the first Acehnese-language magazine, *Majalah Neurôk*, was launched in 2020. A prose translation of the Quran in Acehnese was published on December 13, 2018.

## Language & religion

Acehnese belongs to the Chamic branch of the Malayo-Polynesian branch of the Austronesian language family. Its closest relatives are other Chamic languages, principally spoken in Vietnam and Cambodia. Acehnese is spoken mainly in the northern and western coastal regions of Sumatra and is also spoken by Acehnese descendants in parts of Malaysia, including Kampung Acheh in Kedah.

The language has major dialect groupings named North Acehnese, Pidie, Great Aceh, West Acehnese, and Daya, also called Lamnoe. Further groups include Pasè, Peusangan, Matang, Bueng, Banda Aceh, Meulabôh, Seunagan, and Tunong. Acehnese is written in the Latin script and also has a historical adapted form of the Jawi script called *Jawoe*. The language article describes EBAYD and Husaini’s Spelling as spelling systems.

The vast majority of Acehnese people are Muslims. Earlier traditions included Hinduism and Buddhism, while Sanskrit vocabulary and cultural traces reflect earlier Hindu influence. Islamization followed contact with the Islamic world and was well established in the region by the thirteenth century.
